title: Making Term 4 Terrific
author: Martin Ravindran
summary: Martin Ravindran writes for Australian teachers heading into the final term of the year, arguing that the common excuses about tired students, disruptions and teachers looking ahead to next year should not be allowed to lower standards. He notes that a fact being true does not mean its natural consequence must follow, and that classroom time remains under the teacher's control. He offers four practices: restate and reset routines using retrieval-practice logic, prioritise the present by protecting learning time, celebrate student success to reinvigorate motivation, and pilot one new practice while routines are stable rather than waiting for next year. He cites Greg Ashman's point at ResearchEd Canberra that Term 4 is a good time to pilot changes. The piece closes with four concrete actions teachers can take this week.
points: Treat classroom routines like any retrieval practice: model them again, give praise and corrective feedback, and reteach if needed.
Protecting learning time and focusing on what can be done now reduces both off-task behaviour and teacher anxiety.
Holding high standards in Term 4 creates the opportunity for meaningful praise and a motivating sense of success.
Waiting until next year to fix a weak routine means practising it for ten more weeks, so piloting one change now is better.
The closing checklist gives four practical moves: reset one routine, protect essential learning, revisit earlier work, and trial one manageable change.
quotes: However, there is a stark difference between the reality of a fact and what we do with a fact. It is tempting to think that just because a statement is true, the “natural” consequence is bound to follow.

A routine however, is a learned behaviour, and learning is subject to forgetting. Beginning the term with a review of classroom norms and expectations not only serves a smooth segue from the holidays into the academic term, but sets everyone up for success.

Treat learning time as something to be protected and something that is precious. If needed, remind students (and yourself), that during learning time, the attention and thinking should be on the learning happening in the now.

Continuing to hold high standards and expectations in term 4 may seem counterintuitive to the built-up fatigue of the year, but having these standards grants you the opportunity to give meaningful praise.

If you wait till next year to introduce a new routine that you think would be helpful, or to try a new instructional technique, then you are going to spend the next 10 or so weeks practicing behaviours that you ultimately want replaced. Practice makes permanent, and the longer we stay in the habit of doing something suboptimally, the harder it will be to change.

In Term 4, your students are more likely to be familiar with the routines and practices you already have in place. This makes it a prime opportunity to pilot and test out one new thing, when other things are relatively stable.
Term 4 does not have to be a tired and grueling trudge to the end of the year. It can be an exciting time of consolidation, success and experimentation.
